en: [17v2] Homage to Śrī Herukavajra!
Having bowed to the Lord of Great Bliss for the sake of increasing great bliss, I shall explain various instructions as demonstrated by various masters. [1]
I shall explain the instruction:
by means of the swing and the jewel-thread, [one should practice] at the *mūrdhan* and the *anāhata*.
This instruction on Mahāmudrā, emerged from the Lotus Sprout, is according to the Sūtra. [2] cf.
NSU 1

Through the union with the jewel at the nose, the throbbing bindu situated at the tip of the crest-lock constitutes the instruction on Mahāmudrā; so it has been taught by those who have reached the further shore of reality. [3]
O Hero, like a lotus fiber, unified by means of the swing—
this is the perfectly innate yoga cultivated by Prajñārakṣita. [4]
The animal realm is within the jewel; indeed, there is a single dot (*bindu*) that is without syllables.
This particular jewel of reality was characterized by Nelīpāda: [5] It has the form of a lamp-flame and resides in the center of the moon within the lotus of emanation.
The syllable HŪṂ is the hero who causes melting; this was taught by Ravigupta.
[6] It has the meaning of wisdom (prajñā).
The Caṇḍālī, situated in the center of the navel, is proclaimed by Kṛṣṇācārya;
she is of the nature of the first vowel, possessing the luster of the color of the unstruck (*anāhata*) wisdom.
She is known as Tilakā in the lotus of the navel, while Vasanta resides in the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*).
[The state of] being in union (*vasanta*);
the state of being in union is taught by Kṛṣṇācārya as the becoming of a single flavor (*ekarasa*) of the two. [8] (cf.
NSU 5)
In the center of the two yoni-circles at the navel, it is indicated by the syllable Oṃ;
and in the corners, the four seed-syllables beginning with Locanā are placed by Saraha. [9]
But by means of the non-attachment to emptiness, one attains the inconceivable state.
The practitioner, free from attachment to emptiness,
[should place] the mind at the point between the eyebrows and the nose by means of the guru’s lineage.
One attains the inconceivable reality, which is free from both mind and non-mind.
[10] Rigyrāṃ (?)

The three [energies] that arise from manifestation are like the fire of universal destruction; all these beloved ones of Great Bliss were taught by the noble Nārada. And the cloudless, ever-luminous [state]—such is the doctrine of Kuḍḍāla.
And those by whom it is released for the sake of casting away— yogins directly realize it.
It is considered seedless, always luminous, tranquil, and radiant.
Through the power of meditative cultivation, the wise perceive the stars in the sky.
The mind is the locus of ego-grasping, and the three worlds arise from it;
through the thorough knowledge of reality, the world shall attain non-duality.
This mind is luminous, as are the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving;
through the power of meditation, someone may go to the state of luminosity. [15]
By clearly beholding the moon situated within the lotus of the navel,
one obtains the eye of gnosis, which possesses a quivering pupil.
In the delightful arising of auspicious phenomena, he is radiant with *bindu* and *nāda*;

he is proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa as being in the heart through the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*). The syllable *Aṃ* is in the moon of the womb, and *Hūṃ* is situated in the center of emptiness at the navel.
The syllable *oṃ* is situated in the heart-sun, and *haṃ* is situated in the moon of the head. Through the division into one and many, by way of the sequence of the upper and lower caskets:
The threefold supreme instruction was directly imparted by Bāṇa. [19]
In the center of the eight-petaled lotus at the navel, amidst the petals of the directions, is the radiant seed-syllable Oṃ;
this is what has been taught by the Śabaras and the Kambalas.
One should place a vajra upon a vajra at the navel, within the moon of a lotus; by means of the resonance (*nāda*), one should gradually place the *nāgas* in the sky. [21]
Having manifested the face and meditated upon the syllable *hūṃ* in the trunk,
one should visualize a red syllable *aṃ* in the navel-lotus and a radiant [syllable] at the heart.
In the *Guṇḍārīya-mata*, the wise practitioner should visualize a red drop (*bindu*) resembling a pearl on the thumb-sized penis, and likewise within the navel-lotus. [23]
And one should clearly visualize the moon and sun upon the lotus at the navel, atop each peak;
by means of the resonance from the peak-tips, one shall attain the state of Vajrabhairava.
Alternatively, the peak is at the crown of the head—all this is as previously described.
On the head, O Hero, one should meditate; then they know the world to consist of vajras.
Having pressed the vajra upon the lotus, one must not emit the *bodhicitta*.
One should not transgress the word of the one who is to be sweated (the master), in order to make the three worlds consist of that [nature].
All this is mind-only; the world is like a dream and an illusion.
What wonder is it that the wise, through the power of cultivation, manifest the perfections? [27] The Perfection.
The Madhyamikas know reality to be neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; it is liberated from the four extremes.
That very thought which thinks "it is inconceivable" is itself inconceivable therein; that state is declared to be the absence of thought, like an axe striking a block of wood. [29]

For one who is free from mental agitation: one should meditate upon that which resembles the moon in the sky, within the sphere of the heroic Brahmāṇḍa, arisen from the source of Dharma (dharmodaya), at the end of the ten winds. [30]
But in the *nirmāṇacakra*, she who is said by Mahīdhara to be the Caṇḍālī residing in the wheel of bliss is like the fire of universal destruction (*pralayānala*). [31]
At the navel, within the pericarp situated inside the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), is the Unstruck (anāhata).
The syllables *drā*, *va*, *ka*, *aṅkāra*, and *hūṃ* were proclaimed by the teacher Tattvakaśūri.
In the Vīṇāyātamata, at the navel, the sun and moon are joined by a line and a dot;
at the front, they are encircled by the vowels and consonants, and a white line extends upward from the supreme [point]. [33]

The syllable *vaṃ*, which is the drop of gnosis (*jñānabindu*) devoid of letters and situated in the center of the moon within the emanation-lotus, becomes non-dual when meditated upon by those who have reached the further shore of reality. [34] (cf.
NSU 9)
In the intermediate space, during the emanation, the practitioner of the visualization should count the wind with the red *praṇava* through the mouth by means of ten *śītkāra* sounds.

The wise one should churn with the mouth until non-duality is attained;
the syllables AṂ and HŪṂ were taught by Virūpācārya. [36]
According to the opinion of Nāgabuddhi: From passion (*rāga*), there is no lotus or womb-center;
it is blazing, situated upon the wheel of dharma, the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), unstruck (*anāhata*), and non-dual. [37]
Having fully pervaded the *saṃbhoga* with the syllable *Aṃ*, and having caused it to melt with the tongue, [one should realize] the non-dual, unstruck (*anāhata*) *saṃbhoga*.
Having stepped down and placed it between the lower teeth, Dignāga attained non-duality.
For the sake of accomplishing the Kākatuṇḍī, the wise one should cause the syllable *Aṃ* to dissolve.

[39] One should meditate on a drop (bindu) with the luster of a pearl at the tip of the nose, red and white, through the entry and exit of the syllable *hūṃ*. And having closed his ears, the wise Mātali should not perceive sounds produced by a lute. [40]
Having withdrawn the mind from all directions, one should place the mind within the heart;
then that Lord, having destroyed the darkness of delusion, arises. [41]
To be destroyed. The oral tradition of the path.
For the unsurpassed is non-arising, ineffable, and devoid of intrinsic nature;
it is ineffable, inconceivable, and non-apprehensible—these are the thorns that are equalized. [42]
When one churns the unsurpassed [reality] precisely through the sequence of the downward gate, then one certainly attains the peaceful state that is beyond syllables.
[43] The entire world is firm in syllables; there is nothing at all that is without syllables.
The syllables are dissolved until they become syllable-less.
[44] — [This is] by the venerable Saraha Nīlībhadrapṛṣṭhī.
One should avoid the defects of lethargy, excitement, sloth, and torpor in meditative concentration.
When meditation is free from these defects, then the *mudrā* arises. [45]
When one practices well through yoga by fixing the mind, then I do not perceive the mind; where has it gone, and where could it abide?
[46] Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added.
One should see reality as it truly is; seeing reality, one is liberated.
Through the liberation that is free from conceptual construction, everything arises by itself.
The mantra-practitioner should not cultivate existence, nor should he abandon non-existence.
Mounted upon a lotus fiber, with a radiance like a shimmering drop,
the drop that illuminates within shines like the circle of hair between the eyebrows.
Thus say some.
"Having internalized the world within the body, one who contemplates the *ahaṃkāra* [should place it] in the navel;
the body and *ahaṃkāra* in the *bindu*, and the *bindu* alone as a blaze—thus say others. [50]
Having reflected, "I have no conceptual construction whatsoever," the practitioner attains the unsurpassed state, which is free from the latent impressions of conceptual construction. [51]
Thus say others.
Having reflected, "I have no attachment whatsoever," the knower of yoga [explicitly...]
